newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsican leader sentenced, new bomb attack.
newsitem.headline: Corsican leader sentenced, new bomb attack.

text.p: The leader of the most militant separatist group on the French Mediterranean island of Corsica was sentenced in his absence on Wednesday to a year in jail, of which eight months were suspended.

Francois Santoni, secretary-general of the Cuncolta Naziunalista party, legal facade of the Corsican National Liberation Front - Historical Wing (FLNC), was sentenced by an appeals court for illegal possession of arms.
Just hours after the sentence, a bomb went off in a town whose mayor is an opponent of the separatist cause.
Police said no one was hurt in the late night attack against a civil court building in Ile Rousse whose mayor is Pierre Pasquini, French junior minister for veterans' affairs.
Pasquini's office in the town was the target of an earlier bomb attack on October 4.

Santoni, who will now officially become a fugitive if he fails to surrender, is widely believed to be hiding out in the "maquis," the dense brushland covering much of Corsica, together with his bodyguards.

Santoni's sentence came a week after the hardline FLNC claimed responsibility for a bomb attack at the town hall in the southwest France city of Bordeaux, of which Prime Minister Alain Juppe is mayor.
That attack took place days before the official expiry on Saturday of a truce called by the FLNC. It had already been shattered in recent weeks by dozens of blasts.
The court's sentence followed Santoni's appeal against an earlier sentence on the same arms charges of six months imprisonment, of which five were suspended.
Santoni had argued he had to be armed because he had been the target of assassination attempts by rival groups, including one in May 1995 when one of his bodyguards was killed.
French media widely reported earlier this year that Santoni's group was involved in secret negotiations with the government which apparently later foundered.

The case coincided with publication of a poll which found Corsicans overwhelmingly opposed to independence from France. It also showed approval for Paris's plans to crack down on separatist guerrillas.

Ninety-one percent of those polled by telephone for the Paris weekly L'Evenement du Jeudi opposed independence for the island, racked by two decades of separatist bombings. Just seven percent were in favour.
Successive governments have ruled out independence for the island, whose 250,000 inhabitants rely heavily on subsidies from the mainland.

But the survey found that 61 percent of 500 Corsicans polled by telephone on October 12 did not have confidence in Juppe to find lasting solutions for Corsica. Thirty-seven percent expressed confidence in the premier.
Nevertheless, 82 percent said that they did not believe there was a risk of civil war in Corsica.
